lede: Every state sends MPs to the Lok Sabha based on its population. But seat counts have been frozen on the 1971 census for decades, so fast-growing states have fewer seats than their population suggests. In 2023, Parliament promised women a third of seats, but only after a new census and redrawing of seats, called delimitation. The fight now is over when and how to do both.

players.name: Union government
players.role: Wants to redraw seats and start the women's quota before 2029.

players.name: Opposition parties
players.role: Want the women's quota now, without linking it to new seat maps.

players.name: Southern states
players.role: Fear losing clout because they slowed population growth.

players.name: Delimitation Commission
players.role: A panel led by a Supreme Court judge that redraws constituencies.

players.name: Parliament
players.role: Needs a two-thirds vote to change the Constitution.

timeline.what: Seat counts per state are frozen on the 1971 census, to avoid punishing states that control population.
The last Delimitation Commission redraws constituency borders but keeps each state's seat count the same.
Parliament passes the women's reservation law: one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats, but only after the next census and delimitation.
Bills to raise the seat cap to 850 and start the quota sooner win 298 votes to 230, short of the two-thirds needed.
Reports say the Centre may call a special session late this month to try again. No dates are announced yet.

title: Seats, maps and the women's quota
